Mujahid and al-Hasan take it to mean equality in honouring the sanctuary and performing its rites, with no privilege for its inhabitants. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand it as lodging: anyone may stay wherever he finds room, a view reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, who also cite 'Umar opposing the closing of house doors during the pilgrimage season. On the wrongdoing that makes deviation punishable, Ibn 'Abbas names polytheism, Mujahid and Qatada the worship of other than God, while others name the violation of sacred prohibitions or any sin. Ibn Mas'ud holds that merely intending a sin within the sanctuary is punished, a view Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate, while others hold only the act counts. Al-Tabari judges that the injustice covers every disobedience. Jurists differ on selling and renting houses in Mecca: Abu Hanifa and, in one report, Ahmad forbid it, while al-Shafi'i permits it. Ibn Kathir reports Ahmad's middle position, allowing ownership but forbidding rental.

This verse recalls the favour God bestowed on Ibrahim when He showed him the site of the Sacred House and settled him there, commanding him to build it on monotheism and to purify it from associating partners and from filth. Its purpose is that it be a place for those who circle it, those who stand in worship, and those who bow and prostrate. Commentators explain that the word tubawwi'a means to settle someone or to make the site known, and that the clause "that you associate nothing with Me" clarifies it, since the settlement was meant for worship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that purification primarily means removing association and idol-worship, while others add impurities, blood and false speech. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' take the "standing" to be those who pray, whereas Qatada takes them to be those who stay in Makkah; most scholars hold that these are the worshippers in prayer, whose postures are then listed. On the original building, opinions differ: some report that the House was raised to heaven during the flood and then relocated through a wind or a cloud that revealed its old foundations, while others hold that Ibrahim was the first to build it. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti remain cautious about these narrations, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the prohibition of association is addressed to Ibrahim and to his descendants.

This verse commands Ibrahim to proclaim the pilgrimage to people, who will come on foot and on lean camels from every distant path. Most commentators hold that Ibrahim was the one commanded to call, while al-Hasan held that it was Muhammad, and that those who answered were already in the loins of fathers and wombs of mothers, which is why the talbiya began then, according to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that his voice reached the ends of the earth. The commentators agree that walkers are mentioned first as an honour; Ibn Abbas considered walking the better way, while Malik, al-Shafi'i and most scholars preferred riding after the Prophet's example. On the benefits, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others named trade and the reward of both worlds, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab limited them to the hereafter, and al-Baqir to forgiveness. The known days are, according to different views, the first ten of dhu al-hijja, the days of tashriq, or the day of sacrifice and the days after it. Eating from the offering is, for 'Ata' and Mujahid, a permission, while others made it obligatory, and most scholars call it recommended alongside giving charity. Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas understood the cutting of hair and nails as all the rites, while others limited it to shaving and cleaning. All agree the circumambulation meant is the ifada tawaf. Explanations of the name al-atiq for the House vary between freedom from tyrants and its antiquity.

These verses describe the pilgrimage that God commanded Abraham to proclaim among people, so that they would come to him on foot and on lean camels from every distant road. The commentators explain the purpose of this coming through the phrase "that they may witness benefits for themselves". Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record several opinions: some say the benefits are trade and markets, others forgiveness and reward. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir conclude that the benefits cover both this world and the next, with trade being secondary to the purpose of the pilgrimage, as al-Razi notes.

The commentators agree that the name of God is mentioned at the slaughter of the offerings. On the "known days", Ibn Abbas and most exegetes take them to be the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja, while Malik, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad take them to be the days of sacrifice, and al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari also mention the day of Arafat.

Regarding eating from the offering, the exegetes read the command as permission or recommendation rather than obligation, since people in pre-Islamic times refrained from eating their sacrifices. Al-Shafi'i and most jurists exclude obligatory offerings, while Malik allows eating from some of them. The poor man who is destitute must be fed, and Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima explain who he is. The commentators then take the "removal of dirt" to mean the rites of pilgrimage, such as shaving the head, trimming nails and stoning the pillars, and fulfilling vows to include the slaughter of what was promised. The tawaf al-ifada is identified as the circuit meant by the Ancient House, whose name is explained either by its antiquity or by its protection from tyrants.

This verse describes the final rites of the pilgrimage: after the sacrifice, pilgrims complete their state of consecration by removing the dirt and neglect that accumulated during ihram, by trimming their nails and cutting or shaving their hair, then they fulfil their vows and circumambulate the Ancient House. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'tafath'. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar take it as all the rites of the hajj, Mujahid, 'Ata' and 'Ikrima as trimming the moustache and nails, plucking the armpits, shaving the pubic area and throwing the pebbles, while Qatada and al-Hasan take it as removing the unkempt appearance of ihram, and Abu 'Ubayda and others note that no clear poetic evidence for the word exists. On the vows, Ibn 'Abbas links them to the slaughter of votive camels, Mujahid to the vow of the hajj, to the offering and to any vow made during the pilgrimage, and others to any good deed vowed. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand the circumambulation here as the tawaf al-ifada, a pillar of the hajj that completes the release from ihram, while some, including reports from al-Hasan, understand it as the farewell tawaf. As for the epithet 'ancient', Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid and Qatada explain it as God's liberation of the House from tyrants, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd as its antiquity, and Ibn Jubayr as its rescue from the flood. Al-Tabari prefers the report of Ibn al-Zubayr as the most authentic, while accepting the other meanings as valid.

This verse states that honouring the sacred prohibitions of God, meaning carrying out what He has ordained in the rites and avoiding what He has forbidden, is better for the one who does it in the sight of his Lord, and that grazing livestock is made lawful for you except what is recited to you as forbidden in the Qur'an, such as carrion, blood, pork and what has been dedicated to other than God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the sacred prohibitions to be the rites of the pilgrimage and its sacred places, such as Mecca, the sacred mash'ar and the sacred month, while Mujahid says they include everything God has forbidden, and Ibn Zayd lists the sacred places. Al-Kalbi and others focus on the rites alone. On the abomination of idols, the commentators agree that it means shunning their worship. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the word 'min' as explanatory, meaning the idols that are abomination, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as partitive or indicating the starting point, and Ibn Kathir follows the explanatory reading. As for false speech, Mujahid and Ibn Mas'ud understand it as lies or false testimony, al-Razi and al-Tabari report that it also means polytheism, and al-Zamakhshari mentions arbitrary declarations about what is lawful or unlawful. On the word hunafa', al-Tabari and al-Razi render it as upright or inclining toward truth, while Ibn Juzayy and others render it as pilgrims. The image of the one who associates partners with God, who falls from the sky and is snatched by birds or carried off by the wind, is explained by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Qayyim in both its compound and separate forms, and the narrated hadiths underline the gravity of false testimony.

The commentators explain that the verse commands believers to be sincere toward God, turning away from every false religion toward Islam, and to associate nothing with Him. It then offers an image: whoever associates partners with God is like one who falls from the sky, then is snatched by birds or carried by the wind to a far place from which there is no escape. Most exegetes, including Mujahid, Qatada and al-Tabari, explain that the word sahiq means distant, so the associator is far from guidance. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di take the verse as stating the associator's ruin with no rescue. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari read the image as a compound or divided comparison, in which faith is the sky, associationism the fall, desires the birds and Satan the wind. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi then distinguish the wavering person, pulled apart by many temptations, from the stubborn unbeliever who is settled in error like one lodged in a distant valley. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that hanif can mean both straightness and inclination toward truth, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as sincerity toward God. On the forbidden false speech, most mention false testimony, lying and polytheism, and Ibn Kathir cites a hadith on the subject while noting the weakness of its chain. All place the verse within the context of pilgrimage rites and the honouring of God's symbols.

This verse teaches that honouring the symbols of God, meaning the signs and rites of His religion, springs from the piety of the heart. The commentators broadly agree that the most immediate reference is to the sacrificial animals of the pilgrimage, and that honouring them means choosing animals that are fine, fat and costly, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur extend the term to all the rites of the Hajj, while Ibn Zayd, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and Malik understand the places and markers of the pilgrimage such as Mina, 'Arafat, Muzdalifa, al-Safa and al-Marwa. Al-Hasan, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the symbols to mean the religion's ordinances as a whole. The scholars differ on the benefits of the animals: Mujahid and Qatada say they end once the animal is designated as an offering, whereas 'Ata' allows riding and milking when needed until the sacrifice, a view supported by the hadith of Abu Hurayra cited by al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir. On the place of sacrifice, 'Ata' says Mecca and al-Shafi'i says the whole sacred precinct, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the verse mentions the Ancient House. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the heart is named because it is the seat of piety, and al-Qurtubi notes the Prophet's words that piety is here, pointing to his chest.

This part of the verse says that the sacrificial animals, camels, cattle and sheep brought to the Sacred House, offer the faithful benefits until a set term, and that their place of slaughter is the Ancient House. The commentators largely agree that the 'signs of God' here refer to the offerings, though they differ on details. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak, as transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, hold that the benefits are milk, wool, offspring and riding before the animal is designated as an offering; once it is designated and dedicated, its owner no longer gains anything from it, and that designation is the set term. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, whom al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report as followed by al-Shafi'i, holds instead that after designation the owner may ride the animal or drink its milk when needed, the term then being the slaughter. They rely on reports in which the Prophet told a man leading a camel to ride it. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad allow riding without harm, others restrict it to necessity, and Abu Hanifa forbids it. As for the place of slaughter, most see the whole Sacred Precinct, with Mina included, as the place, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari explain; 'Ata' says it is Mecca, and others point to the circumambulation of ifada. Al-Tabari prefers the view that the offerings are slaughtered within the Haram.

This verse states that God prescribed for every earlier believing community a rite of sacrifice, the shedding of blood to draw near to Him, so that His name would be pronounced over the livestock He had provided. It concludes that your God is one God, so submit to Him alone, and then commands the Prophet to give good tidings to those who humble themselves. The commentators largely agree that manSak refers to the sacrifice, as al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold, although Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir in another report take it to mean a festival, Qatada takes it to mean the pilgrimage, and al-Farra' takes it to mean a customary place of worship. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the purpose is to dedicate the mention of God alone at slaughter, and that only livestock may be offered. The meaning of al-mukhbitin is disputed: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada call them the humble, Mujahid and al-Tabari the tranquil in God, al-Akhfash and al-Hasan the reverent, al-Nakha'i the sincere, al-Kalbi those with tender hearts, and 'Amr ibn Aws those who do no wrong and do not retaliate when wronged. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link these meanings to the idea of lowland, that is, lowering oneself and finding calm, and these readings revolve around two themes, humility and tranquillity in God. The following verses describe these believers as those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned, who endure hardship, who establish prayer and spend from what they have been given.

This verse describes the qualities of the humble (al-mukhbitin), those who lower themselves before their Lord. When God is mentioned their hearts tremble; they are patient in what befalls them; they establish the prayer; and they spend from what God has provided. The commentators agree that these traits express an inner humility and submission. Al-Tabari, quoting Ibn Zayd, explains that the trembling of the heart means that it should not harden. Mujahid takes the humble to be those at rest in God's command, while Ibn Abbas and Qatada call them the modest, al-Akhfash and al-Tabari the lowly and submissive, and Amr ibn Aws those who do no wrong and, when wronged, do not seek revenge. Al-Razi holds that the patience required concerns what comes from God, such as illness and trials, whereas resisting oppressors is an obligation where possible. Ibn Kathir and others apply spending to obligatory charity, support of one's household, and voluntary alms. Ibn Sa'di notes that the particle min indicates a part, showing that what is given is only a small portion of God's provision. On recitation, most read al-muqimi al-salat as a construct, while al-Hasan and Abu Amr read al-salata in the accusative with the nun dropped.

This verse describes camels brought to the Sacred House as among the signs of God's religion, from which pilgrims gain benefit in this world and reward in the next. God commands that His name be mentioned at the slaughter, when the animal stands in line, and once its flanks fall to the ground it may be eaten, with the humble poor who hold back from asking and the one who comes asking given a share. The commentators largely agree that al-Budn are camels. Ibn Kathir reports that Ata, Ibn Umar and al-Hasan extended the term to cows, while Mujahid and the Shafi'is restricted it to camels. Ibn Abbas, al-Razi and others take the good in the verse to be reward in the afterlife, while al-Nakha'i adds that one may ride the animal or drink its milk when in need. The readings of the word sawaff differ: the majority take it to mean standing in ranks, al-Hasan reads sawafi to mean purely dedicated to God, and Ibn Mas'ud reads sawafin, meaning tied at one foreleg. On the two categories of the needy, the scholars differ. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd hold that al-Qani' is the one who asks, while Ikrima and Qatada hold that he is the contented one who does not ask, and Mujahid identifies him as a wealthy neighbour. Al-Tabari prefers the view that al-Qani' is the asker, since al-Mu'tarr is paired with him as a distinct category. The verse concludes that these animals are a favour that calls for gratitude, and that it is not their flesh or blood that reaches God but the piety of the believers.

This verse teaches that what reaches God from the sacrificial animals is not their meat or blood, for God needs nothing, but the piety and sincerity of those who offer them. The commentators report that pre-Islamic Arabs smeared the Ka'ba with the blood of the offerings, and that some Muslims wished to do the same, which this verse forbade. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the meaning is that they will not ascend to God or reach His approval, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand it as meaning that the donors will please Him only through intention, sincerity and the observance of the conditions of piety. All agree that only piety is accepted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take the phrase about glorifying God for guiding you to mean thanking Him for His guidance and pronouncing the basmala and takbir at slaughter, and al-Razi stresses that the glorification concerns God's power. As for the good news for the doers of good, Ibn 'Abbas identifies them as monotheists, others as those who are sincere in all they do, and al-Tabari as those who obey God well. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report a tradition that the verse was revealed about the four caliphs, yet its literal meaning includes every good doer. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the offering aims at the benefit of people, so that the rite is a means rather than an end in itself.

This verse tells the believers that God defends them against the schemes of the polytheists, and that He does not love any treacherous ingrate. The commentators agree that it promises divine protection and gives the reason for it: God does not love those who betray and deny. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand treachery as breaking trusts and covenants, and ingratitude as denying God's blessings, with polytheism as the gravest form of both. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note that the intensive forms of the words describe the polytheists as they truly are.

They differ on the nature of the defence. The reading yudafi'u, followed by most, means for al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi a defence carried out with intensity, like a contest, while Ibn 'Atiyya and others take it simply as defending. Al-Razi observes that the object is left unstated to make the meaning broader, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as answering the believers' wish to know whether God will support them in this world.

Several commentators link the verse to what follows, the permission to fight. According to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir it is the first verse permitting combat, revealed after the Hijra, whereas Muqatil places it before the emigration. For the next verse, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya offer various readings of the defence, including the fighters, the testimony of the upright, and the justice of rulers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi prefer the reading that refers to fighting, and Sayyid Qutb sees a general principle that faith needs strength to protect it.

The commentators explain that God permitted the believers to fight, after a period when they were forbidden to do so, because they had been wronged by the polytheists of Mecca, and that He is able to give them victory. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others report that this is the first verse revealed on permission to fight, linked to the Prophet's emigration from Mecca to Medina; al-Tabari also cites a report that Abu Bakr understood from it that fighting would come. Mujahid, as cited by al-Tabari, holds that it refers to particular believers who were prevented from emigrating. The readings of the verbs differ, and al-Tabari considers their meanings close. On the phrase about God repelling some people by others, opinions vary: al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir understand it as protecting places of worship through struggle, Mujahid as the testimony of upright witnesses, and Ali ibn Abi Talib as the role of the Prophet's companions in protecting those after them. As for the sawami', biya', salawat and masajid, the early scholars differ on which communities they belong to, naming monks, Sabians, Jews, Christians, or the places of worship of earlier religions. All agree that God supports whoever supports His religion, and that all affairs return to Him.

This verse states that God permitted the oppressed believers to fight those who wronged them, namely the emigrants from Mecca who were expelled from their homes for no reason other than saying 'Our Lord is God'. Commentators regard it as one of the first verses on permission to fight, and they cite the words of Abu Bakr and Ibn Abbas about its occasion. Most agree that 'the repelling' means God setting some people against others, so that the Muslims' struggle against the idolaters prevents the latter from destroying places of worship. Others take it as repelling injustice through testimony, the justice of rulers or retaliation, but al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi find fighting more fitting to the context. As for the places of worship, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak identify the sawami' with monks' hermitages, the biya with Christian churches, the salawat with Jewish synagogues and the mosques with Muslim prayer halls, while Qatada takes the sawami' to be those of the Sabians and Abu al-'Aliya takes the salawat to be Sabian places of prayer. Ibn Zayd understands the salawat as the prayers of the Muslims, which cease when an enemy invades. Readers differ on the pronunciation of 'lahuddimat', and exegetes debate whether the pronoun in 'where the name of God is much mentioned' refers only to the mosques or to all of them; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the broader meaning. The verse ends with the promise that God will help whoever helps Him, which most take as support for the religion, while the description of those established in power is applied by al-Razi and others to the emigrants or to just rulers.

This verse describes those whom God establishes on earth: they keep up the prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and the final outcome of all matters belongs to God. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, understand it first of the Companions of the Prophet, the emigrants who were wrongfully driven from their homes and then established by God. Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya take it to cover the whole community. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also record other readings: the four rightly guided caliphs, the rulers, the people who observe the five prayers, or the emigrants, the Helpers and their followers. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud use it as evidence for the legitimacy of the rightly guided caliphs, and al-Zamakhshari cites 'Uthman's saying: "By God, this is praise before the trial." Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a reminder to give thanks for the gift of victory. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain "establishing" as victory over enemies. Al-Sa'di understands it as real authority and the power to enforce decisions, and treats prayer, zakat, enjoining good and forbidding evil as the foundations of a sound society. On "the outcome of affairs," all agree that it returns to God alone, who will reward and punish on the Day of Judgment. The verse belongs to a passage consoling the Prophet ﷺ over his people's rejection.

This verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ over his people's denial: before the Quraysh, other nations denied their messengers too, namely the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the people of Lot, the people of Madyan, and Pharaoh who denied Moses despite his clear signs. The commentators explain that God gave these disbelievers respite before seizing them, and that the question « how was My rejection? » expresses astonishment and affirmation: God turned their blessings into affliction, their life into destruction and their prosperity into ruin. They agree that Moses' own people did not deny him; it was the Copts, which is why the verb is in the passive. The following verses cite ruined towns. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that « fallen upon its roofs » means its walls collapsed onto its ceilings, and that the abandoned well is one left without people. For the « lofty palace », ʿIkrima, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ understand a plastered building, while Qatada and al-Dahhak understand a tall one; al-Tabari favours the first, since shid means plaster in Arabic. Ibn Kathir considers these views complementary rather than contradictory. Several scholars, including Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada, place these ruins in Yemen or Hadramawt, without agreeing on the exact site. The general lesson they draw is to travel the earth and reflect, for true blindness is the blindness of the heart.

Verse 43 of Surat al-Hajj names the people of Abraham and the people of Lot among the nations that called their prophets liars. It belongs to a passage of consolation for the Prophet ﷺ when his own people reject him. The commentators explain that these earlier nations treated their messengers the same way, so the Prophet should not be grieved. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others count these peoples among those whom God gave respite before punishing them. Al-Tabari defines this respite (imla') as delaying the punishment although God could have hastened it. Most exegetes give no details on the destruction of the people of Abraham and Lot here, and only allude to them while recalling God's way with those who deny. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qasimi note that the verse does not say 'the people of Moses', because his people, the Children of Israel, did not deny him; it was the Copts who did. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the people of Abraham resemble the Quraysh in harming and driving out their prophet, which explains their mention right after the expulsion of the believers. Overall, the commentators agree on the apparent meaning of the verse, which aims at consolation and warning.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ by recalling the nations who denied their messengers before the Quraysh: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the people of Lot, and the people of Madyan, then Moses. Commentators note that the passive wording « and Moses was denied » indicates that his own people, the Children of Israel, did not deny him, and that it was the Copts who did so. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi see in this also an emphasis on how shameful the denial was, given how clear his signs were. Most explain « I gave the disbelievers respite » as a postponement of punishment, and « then how was My rejection? » as a rhetorical question affirming the severity of God's retribution, which turned blessings into ruin. Al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take the respite as a way of letting the wrongdoers go further, while Ibn Kathir reports that God gives the wrongdoer time before seizing him. In the next verse, the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, understand that the town lies fallen upon its roofs and that the abandoned well has no one left to draw water. About the lofty castle, al-Tabari, Ikrima, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr take it to mean a palace coated with plaster, while Qatada and al-Dahhak take it to mean a high building, and al-Tabari prefers the plaster sense while noting that the meanings converge. Several commentators, including al-Biqa'i and Ibn Kathir, draw from these ruins a call to travel the earth and reflect, since it is the hearts, not the eyes, that go blind.

This verse describes many towns that God destroyed because their people were wrongdoers, meaning they disbelieved and rejected their messengers. Their houses lie fallen upon their roofs, their wells stand abandoned with no one drawing water, and their lofty palaces are empty. The commentators agree that "town" here means its people, and that khawiya means ruined, collapsed, or emptied of its inhabitants. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain "upon their roofs" as the roofs having fallen first and the walls then collapsing on top of them, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi allow that the walls may still stand while the homes are empty. On the abandoned well, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada say it is one left with no people, while others take it as a dried-up well or one stripped of its buckets and ropes. As for the lofty palace, most, including Ikrima, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, read mashid as plastered with lime, whereas Qatada, al-Dahhak and Muqatil take it as high and tall, and al-Kalbi as strongly fortified. Al-Tabari judges the lime reading the most correct, supporting it with Arabic poetry. Several authors report that this well and palace were in Hadramawt or Yemen and belonged to ancient peoples such as the people of Salih or 'Ad, though Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan reject that location. All of them present these ruins as a lesson, and they note that true sight is the sight of the heart.

God urges the disbelievers of Mecca to travel through the earth and look at the ruins of earlier nations who denied their messengers, so that their hearts may understand the lesson and their ears may hear the warnings. The commentators agree that the hearts are to grasp what must be understood of monotheism and the ears what must be heard of revelation, and that the harmful blindness is blindness of the heart to the truth, not of the eyes. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi see the mention of the breasts as emphasis or as a means of fixing where this blindness lies, much like saying they speak with their mouths, while al-Jalalayn treats it as mere emphasis. Mujahid says every person has four eyes, two in the head for this world and two in the heart for the hereafter, a view cited by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi. Al-Tabari, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi take the verse to show that reason resides in the heart, a view the philosophers reject, while al-Alusi holds that both heart and brain take part in knowing. Some reports link the verse to the blind companion Ibn Umm Maktum, though al-Alusi questions the soundness of that report.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that the disbelievers mockingly urge him to hasten the punishment he threatens them with, but God does not break His promise: the punishment will certainly come, and God brought it upon them at Badr, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi. As for the phrase 'a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count', the commentators differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima took it to mean a day of the Hereafter, and Ibn 'Abbas in another report a day of the six days in which God created the heavens and the earth. Al-Tabari judged it closer to the truth that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, and that God does not hasten punishment but grants respite. Others explain that the verse describes how long and harsh the punishment is, since days of hardship seem long, as al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Razi state, the latter holding that a wise person should not desire the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as showing God's patience and power, for one day and a thousand years are equal to Him. The commentators agree that the next verse, 'how many a town I gave respite while it was wrongdoing, then I seized it', shows that God grants the wrongdoers a delay before seizing them, and that all return to Him.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, consoling him over the impatience of the idolaters who demanded the punishment. It states that God grants respite to unjust towns without hastening their punishment, then seizes them, and that all return is to Him. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di, take "the town" to mean its people, and its injustice to be polytheism and disbelief. The respite (imla') is understood as a delay accompanied by the intention to punish. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the verse uses "wa" (and) rather than "fa" (then), as in the preceding verse, because this clause continues the series of sentences joined by "wa", whereas the earlier verse stands in apposition to a previous clause. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the purpose is to remind the idolaters that postponing a threat does not cancel it. The disputes over the "day with your Lord like a thousand years" concern the preceding verse. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that the real punishment awaits disbelievers in the hereafter, and that the seizing by God is a severe punishment.

God tells His Prophet to say to all people that he is only a clear warner, having no power to hasten or delay the punishment, which lies with God alone. The commentators place the verse in the context of unbelievers who mockingly demanded that the punishment be hastened. They note that God gives respite to unjust towns before seizing them, and that all will return to Him. The verse then contrasts two groups: those who believe and do good deeds, who will receive forgiveness and a generous provision, which most identify as Paradise, and those who strive against God's signs, who are the companions of the Blazing Fire. The exegetes agree that the address is primarily to the polytheists, and that the mention of believers and their reward is meant to vex the unbelievers or to encourage the faithful. The word mu'ajjizin is read differently: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the doubled form, meaning those who discourage people from faith, as held by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn al-Zubayr, while the others read the form with an alif, which Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj understood as opposing, contending against, or thinking they could escape God. Al-Tabari judged both readings close in meaning and both correct. Al-Zamakhshari explained that the alif form is borrowed from racing, each contestant trying to outpace the other. Ibn 'Atiyya and others mention the account of the Gharaniq, which some scholars reject.

The commentators explain that this verse follows passages about God granting respite to the wrongdoers before their punishment. God commands His Prophet to tell all people that he is a plain and clear warner, and that the timing of punishment is not in his hands, either to hasten or to delay. God then divides people into two groups. Those who believe and do righteous deeds will receive forgiveness for their past sins and a generous provision, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify as Paradise, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe it as an enduring and excellent reward. Those who strive against Our signs to frustrate them will be the companions of the Blazing Fire.

The main disagreement concerns the word "mu'ajizin". Read with an alif, as in the majority reading, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean opposing and contending, al-Farra' takes it as hostility, and Qatada and al-Zajjaj explain it as the disbelievers thinking they could escape God. In the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, "mu'jizin", Mujahid and Ibn al-Zubayr understand it as discouraging people from following the Prophet, while al-Sudi takes it as making the believers appear weak.

Al-Tabari concludes that both readings are close in meaning, since whoever is powerless before God's signs is in effect challenging God. Ibn Atiyya argues that explaining the word as thinking one can overcome God goes beyond the wording itself.

This verse closes a passage in which God tells His Prophet ﷺ to say to the people that he is only a clear warner, with no power to hasten or delay the punishment, which belongs to God alone. Those who believe and do good deeds receive forgiveness and a generous provision, which most commentators identify as Paradise. As for those who strive against God's signs, meaning the Quran and the evidence of the message, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire. The commentators agree on the general sense: these are opponents who work to nullify the revelation. They differ, however, on the wording and meaning of the word mu'ajizin. In the majority reading with an alif, Ibn Abbas, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj explain it as opposition, rivalry, or thinking one can outwit God, and Qatada adds that they believed they could escape God. In the reading with a doubled jim attributed to Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, Mujahid explains it as discouraging people from following the Prophet. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are close in meaning, since rejecting God's signs amounts to challenging God. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi stress the idea of competition. Al-Mawardi reports that some understood the striving as denial of the Quran and others as obstinacy. Al-Razi holds that the striving was mainly directed at the Prophet and the believers, since one cannot truly overcome God. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn describe the Jahim as the blazing fire of lasting punishment.

This verse states that before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, Allah sent no messenger or prophet without Satan casting something into his wish or recitation when he recited; Allah then annuls what Satan cast and firmly establishes His verses. The commentators generally distinguish the messenger, who was sent with a scripture or law, from the prophet, a broader category, although some, such as al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and the Mu'tazilites, treat them as equivalent. As for the word tamanna, most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, take it to mean recited, so the intrusion occurred during the recitation; others read it as speaking or as desiring the guidance of one's people. Many commentators relate the Gharaniq story as the occasion of revelation, but Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Hajar, among others, consider its chains unreliable, and scholars such as al-Qadi 'Iyad, al-Razi and al-Alusi reject it as incompatible with the prophets' infallibility. Some hold that the intrusion came into the listeners' ears or through a voice imitating the Prophet's, while others hold it was a slip of the tongue. All agree that this trial exposes hearts: those with sickness or doubt and hypocrisy, and the hardened hearts, namely the polytheists, go further astray, while those given knowledge gain in faith and humility. The commentators also agree that God guides the believers to the straight path and that the disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes or the punishment of a barren day, which some identify as the day of Badr and others as the Day of Resurrection.

This part of the verse explains that God made what Satan casts into the Prophet's recitation a trial for those whose hearts have a sickness, meaning doubt and hypocrisy, and for those whose hearts are hardened and do not yield to the truth, namely the polytheists. Most commentators understand the casting as a phrase inserted into the Prophet's recitation, 'These are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for'. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud relate the well-known story of the occasion of revelation, but Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and al-Suyuti note that all its chains of transmission are broken or weak. al-Razi rejects it at length and treats it as a late invention. al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that what is cast is a suggestion or confusion in minds, which God then cancels. al-Qurtubi, al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur accept that the Prophet may have been misled in his recitation while remaining protected in transmitting revelation. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di draw from the passage a lesson about three kinds of hearts: the sound heart that rejects error, the sick heart that wavers, and the hard heart that persists. According to al-Zamakhshari, the 'wrongdoers' are the hypocrites and the polytheists, and the 'far-reaching schism' is an opposition with no return. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the distance to mean deep misguidance.

This verse links two truths: God makes clear to those who have knowledge that the Qur'an is the truth from their Lord, and He guides those who believe to the straight path. Most commentators take the pronoun in 'that it is the truth from your Lord' to refer to the Qur'an, so that those with knowledge recognise it as God's word, their faith is strengthened and their hearts become humble before it. Al-Tabari also reads the verse as covering the abrogation of what Satan had cast and the firming up of the verses that follow, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand 'those given knowledge' as the believers of this community. On the closing phrase, al-Tabari takes it as God's guidance to the clear truth, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi read it as guidance to sound reasoning that reaches the truth in ambiguous matters. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes three kinds of heart: the sound and humble, the dead and hardened, and the sick, pulled between two tendencies, with trial revealing what each carries. The widely told account of the 'exalted cranes' linked to this passage is rejected by several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qadi Iyad, al-Razi, Ibn Ashur and Muhammad Abduh, who find its chains weak or its content incompatible with prophetic infallibility, so it is not used as a basis for interpretation. The commentators generally read the passage as consolation for the Prophet and as a statement of God's established practice regarding the messengers. Those who disbelieve remain in doubt until the Hour or the barren day overtakes them.

This verse states that those who disbelieve will remain in doubt about the Qur'an, that is, about this revelation, until the Hour comes upon them suddenly or the punishment of a barren day reaches them. Commentators differ on what the pronoun "about it" refers to. Al-Tabari, who chooses this view, follows Ibn Jurayj in taking it to be the Qur'an, as do Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd take it to mean what Satan cast, while others take it to mean the Prophet or the religion. As for "the Hour", most identify it with the Day of Resurrection, though al-Hasan and others say it refers to each person's death. The "barren day" has two main interpretations. The first, held by Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and chosen by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, is the Day of Badr. It is called barren because the disbelievers gained nothing from it, because they were killed before evening, or because angels fought in it. The second, held by al-Dahhak, 'Ikrima and al-Hasan, is the Day of Resurrection, a day with no night after it. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Shinqiti consider this the stronger view, while accepting that Badr was among the things they had been warned of. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi also note that the day may refer to the day of defeat, and in every reading the verse is a warning. The general meaning is the same in all cases: their doubt will persist until the punishment overtakes them.

This part of the verse declares that sovereignty on that Day belongs to God alone, with no rival, and that He judges among His creatures by their deeds: those who believed and did righteous deeds will dwell in gardens of bliss, while those who disbelieved and denied Our signs will face a humiliating punishment. The commentators agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take the Day to be the Resurrection, and Ibn Kathir calls this the sound view. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, however, allow that the barren day may be the Day of Badr, linking the verse to the doubt of the disbelievers mentioned just before it. Ibn 'Atiyya considers both readings valid, since they preserve the force of the disjunction 'or'. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Baydawi explain the word 'barren' as a day of slaughter, a day without good, or a day without equal. In the following verse, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the goodly provision refers to the reward of the martyrs or to Paradise, and that the one slain and the one who dies in God's cause are equal in reward, while Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the Law holds the slain to be more excellent.

This part of the verse describes the fate of those who disbelieved and denied Our signs: they will suffer a humiliating punishment. The commentators connect it to the Day when sovereignty belongs to God alone, who will judge between people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain that disbelief is the heart's refusal of the truth, together with rejecting its signs and being arrogant towards the messengers. Al-Baydawi notes that the particle fa is used for the disbelievers to show that their punishment results from their deeds, whereas the reward of believers is a favour from God. Al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the word muhin means humiliating, and that the punishment includes what degrades those who suffer it. Some link the verse to the day of Badr, while al-Qurtubi regards this reading as possible without insisting on it. The following verses, discussed by several commentators including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, speak of the reward of emigrants who were killed or died in God's way. Al-Tabari reports that some Companions considered the slain and the one who died to be equal in merit, while others preferred the slain. The overall reading thus stresses God's justice in the final judgement, between the reward of believers and the punishment of those who rejected the revelation.

This verse promises that those who emigrated in the cause of Allah, whether they were killed in battle or died in their beds, will be given a goodly provision by Allah, which most commentators understand as the everlasting delights of Paradise, and that Allah is the best of providers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di affirm that the reward of one who dies while emigrating is due from Allah, as stated in the verse of an-Nisa'. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the equal treatment in the promise reflects the shared intention and root of the deed.

The commentators relate the occasion of revelation: when Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salama died, some people said that those killed among the emigrants are superior to those who died naturally, and the verse placed them on an equal footing. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi cite in this context the report of Fadala ibn Ubayd about two funerals. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the wider sharia view holds the slain to be superior, while others, including al-Qurtubi citing Ibn al-Mubarak, consider the two equal in merit, and al-Razi cites a hadith of Anas describing them as partners in reward.

As to the meaning of the goodly provision, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take it as the bounties of Paradise, and al-Tabari also allows the provision of martyrs in the intermediate state. Ibn Juzayy judges the Paradise reading the stronger one, since it covers both martyrs and the dead. Ibn 'Abbas took it to mean lawful sustenance, al-Kalbi war booty, and al-Asamm knowledge and understanding, views that al-Razi and al-Baydawi regard as weak. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan observe that the verse does not specify rank, and the promise of provision does not by itself imply a difference in what is given.

This verse states that Allah will admit those who emigrated in His cause and were then killed or died into an abode that will please them, namely Paradise with its delights that no eye has seen and no ear has heard. The commentators note that God knows the intentions and deeds of the emigrants and is forbearing, not hastening punishment. Most agree that the emigrants are those who left Mecca for Medina, and that the verse places the one killed and the one who dies naturally on equal footing in the promise, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi report. Ibn Kathir recounts how Fadala ibn Ubayd said he did not mind in which of the two graves he would be raised, relying on this verse.

On whether one is superior to the other, opinions differ. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the verse does not establish equal merit, only equal provision, and that the revealed law shows the one who was killed to be more excellent, a view al-Qurtubi also reports. Others, as al-Qurtubi notes, regard both the slain and the one who dies in God's cause as martyrs, with the slain having a distinction for what he suffered for God's sake. Ibn 'Atiyya points out that equality in the promise does not mean equality in rank. On the 'goodly provision', al-Kalbi takes it to be spoils of war, al-Asamm knowledge, while most take it as Paradise's reward or the martyrs' provision in the barzakh.

The commentators link to this passage verses on retaliation and divine aid. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that it was revealed concerning Muslims attacked during the sacred months and then granted victory. Ibn Jurayj understands it as referring to the polytheists who persecuted the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Mawardi and al-Shawkani explain that divine victory means triumph and dominance in this world and proof by argument in the next.

The commentators explain that this verse sets out the right of someone who has been wronged to repay the wrong in kind, and that if he is attacked again after that, God will support him, for God is Pardoning and Forgiving. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that whoever retaliates against his aggressor to the same degree and is then wronged again will be helped by God. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi note that the word "punishment" used for the first response is employed for the sake of verbal correspondence, and that the real meaning is a just retaliation without excess.

Regarding the end of the verse, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud see in it a subtle encouragement to pardon, which is better, and proof that God is able to punish, since only one who has the power to punish can be described as Pardoning. Ibn 'Ashur links this limit to the measure of retaliation: the response must be proportionate to the harm suffered.

Opinions differ mainly on the occasion of revelation. Ibn Jurayj, al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy connect it to the Meccan polytheists who persecuted the Prophet and drove him out. Muqatil, as reported by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, links it instead to a fight that took place in a sacred month. Al-Mawardi mentions another view, according to which it concerns the polytheists who mutilated the Muslims killed at Uhud. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur relate it to the broader passage on the right to self-defence.

The commentators explain that "that" refers to the victory promised to the wronged, and that this victory comes from God's complete power. One sign of that power is that He causes the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night, meaning that He adds to one what the other loses in hours, or that the darkness of one enters the place of the light of the other as the sun sets and rises, just as a house is lit by a lamp and goes dark when it is removed. Al-Zamakhshari reports both meanings, and al-Shinqiti finds the first more apparent and more widely held. All stress that God hears the words of His servants and sees their deeds, and nothing escapes Him.

Most exegetes connect the verse to what precedes it: the power that alternates night and day is proof of the ability to grant victory. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur also see a hint that fortunes alternate, so that the defeated may become victorious, and Ibn 'Ashur notes the subtlety of the metaphor, since the retreat of darkness and light happens gradually.

The next clause, "that is because God is the Truth," is read differently. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Mawardi report from Yahya ibn Salam that al-Haqq is one of God's names, while others take it to mean the possessor of truth or that His worship is true. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand it as the real God alone deserving worship. As for falsehood, al-Hasan takes it to mean the idols, while Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj take it to mean Satan. The readings differ between ya and ta in "yad'un," and al-Tabari prefers the ya.

This part of the verse states that God is the Truth that endures, that whatever is worshipped besides Him, whether idols or rival deities, is false and can neither harm nor benefit, and that He is the Most High over His creation through His power and dominion, the Great in His essence, attributes and sovereignty, so that nothing is greater than Him. Most commentators connect the word "that" to the preceding passage, which concerns God's power over the alternation of night and day and His knowledge of speech and deeds, or the support given to those who were wronged. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God is the true deity, the only one deserving worship because He holds absolute authority, whereas what is invoked besides Him is void and cannot harm or benefit. On the meaning of "al-Haqq", opinions differ: Yahya ibn Salam took it as one of God's names, Ibn 'Isa as "the Possessor of truth", and al-Suddi as "His worship is true"; al-Sam'ani and al-Qurtubi lean toward "the Possessor of right". As for "the false", al-Hasan identified it with idols, Qatada with Iblis, and Ibn Juraij with Satan, while many exegetes prefer the general sense of everything worshipped apart from God. The two readings, "tad'un" and "yad'un", are both recorded, al-Tabari preferring the form with ya. All agree that "al-'Aliyy" means the One who is exalted above all by His power, and "al-Kabir" the Great beyond whom nothing is greater. Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi note that these epithets express the completeness of the divine essence, and al-Razi observes that they affirm the perfection of God's power.

This verse draws attention to the blessing of rain: God sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green. The commentators read it as proof of God's complete power, since the One who revives the earth after its death can also resurrect the dead, as al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti note. They agree that the verb "tusbihu" is in the nominative because it is coordinated with the sending down of water, not an answer to the question; in the subjunctive the meaning would reverse into denying the greening, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain. On the meaning of "tusbihu", Ibn 'Atiyya and Ikrima take it to refer to the morning after a rainy night, holding that greening happens only in Mecca and Tihama. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir, read it as "becomes", so the greening applies to every land and may come some time after the rain. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the imperfect tense conveys the lasting effect of the rain over time. On the closing words "Lattif Khabir", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi say God is gentle in providing sustenance to his servants and knows their despair when rain is delayed, while others point to the subtlety with which plants are drawn out of the soil and to God's knowledge of human needs. No legal ruling is drawn from this verse.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms God's absolute ownership of everything in the heavens and on earth, in creation, possession and governance, all of it being His servants and property with no partner. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it to mean that all creatures are in need of Him, while He is free of need of them, and that He is worthy of praise among His servants for His bounties. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that He deserves praise for His attributes and actions. Al-Nasafi adds that His self-sufficiency will continue even after what is in the heavens and on earth perishes, and that His praise precedes the praise of any creature. Ibn 'Ashur explains that stressing God's self-sufficiency shows that idols, which depend on others to be made and moved, cannot be divine. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan connect the verse to the mention of rain and the greening of the earth, which display God's subtlety and knowledge. Al-Razi reads the surrounding context as a reminder of divine power. The commentators agree that the verse recalls God's sovereignty, self-sufficiency and praiseworthiness, and that this grounds His oneness and the rejection of worshipping anything other than Him.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds people of God's blessings: He has made subservient to them what is on the earth, including animals, crops, fruits and minerals, and has made ships run on the sea by His command. It is He who holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission, and all of this is part of His kindness and mercy towards mankind. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di, agree that subjection means making these things docile and available for human benefit, and that holding up the sky is one of God's gentle acts towards His servants. The exception "except by His permission" is understood by many as referring to the Day of Resurrection or to the divine will. They differ on some details: al-Tabari and al-Nasafi link the ships to "what is on the earth" and so to the subjection, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that they are singled out because their subjection is remarkable. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi also allow that "except by His permission" may refer to the holding itself. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti widen the subjection to animals, minerals and natural forces, and read the holding of the sky as the control of rain, lightning and celestial bodies. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi distinguish ra'fa, which averts harm, from rahma, which brings benefit. The verse ends by noting that man is ungrateful for these blessings.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds people of God's power and blessings: it is He who gave life to humans when they were nothing, who causes them to die at the end of their term, and who will raise them on the Day of Resurrection for judgement, yet humans remain ungrateful for these favours. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi agree that the first giving of life is creation and the second is resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy hold that the first giving of life includes the breathing of the soul, and that the death mentioned is ordinary death. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a conclusion drawn from the earlier proofs of resurrection. Al-Shinqiti counts two lives and two deaths, the first being in the mother's womb before the soul is breathed in. As for 'man', Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean the disbeliever, and some cite named leaders of Quraysh, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Nasafi extend it to the human species or most of it. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that ingratitude is the common trait of people. In the surrounding context, al-Tabari understands the favours as the subjection of land creatures and ships and the holding up of the sky, and the ungrateful one as the one who associates others with God. Al-Sha'rawi notes that no one has ever claimed to create, which grounds belief in resurrection.

This verse states that God has appointed for every community a rite that it observes, so the idolaters should not dispute the Prophet on this matter, and he should call to his Lord, for he is on a straight guidance. The commentators differ on the meaning of manasik. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Qutayba understand it as a festival, al-Dahhak as a place of slaughter, while al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it as sacrifice or the places of the rites of pilgrimage. Al-Tabari prefers the shedding of blood during the days of sacrifice at Mina, since the dispute concerned sacrificial animals. Al-Hasan and al-Razi understand it as worship or sacred law in general, and al-Razi considers this the closest meaning, citing the verse that Dhe gave each of you a law and a way. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Abu al-Su'ud see the laws as sharing a common basis while differing in details. Regarding the prohibition, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say it instructs the Prophet not to heed their objections, al-Zajjaj says it forbids him to argue with them, and Ibn Juzayy explains that the truth is too clear to be contested. Ibn Atiyya reports that the verse was revealed over a dispute about eating slaughtered animals, while Ibn Ashur links the dispute to the pilgrimage rites and to monotheism. Ibn Atiyya and al-Shawkani note that the conciliatory command in the next verse is considered abrogated by the verse of the sword. The shared message is steadfastness in calling to God.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ on how to respond when the disbelievers argue with him after the truth has become clear and the proof has been established. He tells him to say that God knows best what they do, meaning their disbelief and denial, and that He will requite them for it. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that the Prophet should turn away from such disputes and leave the matter to God, who will judge between truth and falsehood on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they disputed. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, links the argument to sacrifices: the polytheists said that what God had slaughtered should not be eaten, while what the believers slaughtered was lawful. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Wahidi mention a similar context involving the Quraysh and Khuza'a over slaughter. Ibn 'Atiyya gives the same occasion but holds that the instruction to remain steadfast is a mere truce abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view also taken by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Razi reads the verse as firm and as meaning that one should not engage in fruitless controversy, and he suggests it may concern the hypocrites, an opinion Ibn al-Jawzi also records. Most commentators see here a lesson in conduct: do not answer those who dispute in bad faith, and entrust the matter to God.

This part of the verse states that on the Day of Resurrection God will judge between believers and disbelievers concerning what they disputed in matters of religion, so that truth will be separated from falsehood. The commentators agree that the address includes both groups and that its purpose is to console the Prophet ﷺ for what his opponents inflicted on him. The judgment will bring reward and punishment, just as the signs and proofs had settled matters in this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi explain that the disagreement means each side holding the opposite of what the other holds, and al-Baghawi and the Jalalayn give the same sense. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur add that the dispute may have concerned the slaughter of animals.

Many scholars link the verse to what precedes it. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, and Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani describe the polytheists' argument over animals slaughtered by Muslims and the eating of carrion. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Ashur see this as the occasion of the verses on rites. Al-Razi gives several meanings of the word manasik, namely festival, sacrifice and revealed law, and prefers the last. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy hold that the verse of conciliation was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi, citing Ibn al-Jawzi, considers it still valid for the hypocrites. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read it mainly as an instruction not to be diverted from one's mission by disputation.

This verse affirms that Allah's knowledge encompasses everything in the heavens and the earth, that nothing is hidden from Him, that this knowledge is recorded in a Book, and that doing so is easy for Him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, identify this Book as the Preserved Tablet, in which Allah recorded everything that will occur until the Day of Resurrection before creation. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the pen, and al-Tabari reports views from Ibn Abbas and Ka'b al-Ahbar. As for what "that" refers to, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as the recording in the Tablet, while Ibn Juzayy links it to the judgment between the parties and Ibn Jurayj to the judgment on the Last Day. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi accept several readings together: the knowledge, the recording and the judgment. Al-Razi and al-Jalalayn read the verse as an affirmation of divine knowledge. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as consolation for the Prophet, and the Book as an image conveying comprehensive knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that knowing and recording these matters is easy for the Knower in His essence, a point al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan discuss critically. All commentators place the verse in the context of the dispute with the polytheists and see it as the basis for the divine judgment to come on the Day of Resurrection.

This part of the verse says that the idolaters worship, besides God, things for which God has sent down no authority (sultan), of which they have no knowledge, and that the wrongdoers have no helper to shield them from God's punishment. Most commentators understand sultan as proof or argument, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi state. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that this worship rests neither on revelation nor on evident reason. Al-Razi builds on these two notions to argue that a polytheist may be in error without knowing it, and that blind imitation is condemned. Ibn Kathir adds that this belief was inherited from the forefathers and was made attractive by Satan. For the closing phrase, al-Razi gives two readings of nasir: help in this world, or the absence of any valid argument for their faith, and he notes that the Mu'tazilites use it to deny intercession. Ibn 'Ashur holds that 'the wrongdoers' refers to the idolaters, while Ibn Sa'di reads it as meaning that nothing rescues them from divine punishment. Al-Sha'rawi distinguishes compelling power from proof, and observes that the verse does not deny their victory but the absence of anyone who would come to their support.

This verse describes the reaction of the disbelievers of Quraysh when the clear verses of the Quran are recited to them: their faces show disgust, and they almost lash out at those who recite them. God then tells His Prophet to announce something worse: the Fire, which God has promised to the disbelievers, and what a miserable destination it is. The commentators largely agree on the basic meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Muhammad ibn Ka'b explain that yasṭūna means to attack, to seize with the hands or to fall upon someone, and that these meanings come to the same thing. Al-Tabari transmits these readings, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take al-munkar as the revulsion and anger visible on their faces, or as the denial itself. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as an image of anger overflowing from the heart. On what the 'worse thing' refers to, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as the disbelievers' rage at the reciters and the distress they feel, whereas al-Razi prefers their intention to harm their opponents, since their final fate is the eternal Fire. The readers differ on the word 'the Fire' (nominative, accusative or genitive), each with its grammatical justification. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that God's promise may mean that He threatened them with this punishment, or that He promised the Fire its prey. Al-Qasimi, al-Sha'rawi and Ibn Sa'di stress the ironic tone of the expression.

In this verse God addresses mankind and offers a parable that calls for careful listening and reflection: the idols and rivals that people invoke besides God cannot create even a fly, not even if they all combined their powers, and if a fly snatches something from them they cannot get it back. Both the seeker and the sought are thus weak. The commentators report that the verse targets the idols around the Kaaba and serves to expose the polytheists' ignorance and belittle their gods. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the fly is chosen for its insignificance, weakness, repulsiveness and multitude, and that the inability to create it reveals all the more the powerlessness before what is greater. Ibn 'Abbas and others report that the pagans smeared the idols with saffron or honey, and flies settled on them; al-Sudi says they placed food before the idols which the flies ate.

Scholars differ on who is the seeker and who is the sought. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the idol as the seeker and the fly as the sought; al-Sudi and al-Dahhak take the worshipper as the seeker and the deity as the sought; others reverse the roles, making the fly the seeker. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the phrase equates the two in weakness, though the idol is in fact weaker still, being inert. Al-Razi treats the argument as refuting the claim that these idols are divine, and he distinguishes between proofs concerning creation and those concerning deserved worship. On the phrase 'they did not measure God with His due measure', the commentators read it as meaning that they neither magnified nor truly knew Him as He deserves. The verse closes by affirming that God is strong and mighty, unopposed.

This verse states that the idolaters did not truly measure God by His due, since they associate with Him idols that cannot create a fly nor recover what a fly takes from them. The commentators explain the verb qadarū in several ways: al-Farra' takes it to mean glorifying God as He deserves, al-Akhfash to mean truly knowing Him, and Qutrub to mean describing Him as He should be described. The verse closes with two attributes, strength and might, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take as a rebuttal of polytheism: the One who is strong and unassailable cannot have a weak and vanquished partner. Ibn 'Ashur presents this closing sentence as a warning of punishment. On who the seeker and the sought are in the preceding verse, the views differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the idol as the seeker and the fly as the sought, whereas al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take the worshipper as the seeker and the worshipped idol as the sought, and Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan record several readings. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi also report a tradition that the verse was revealed about the Jews of Medina who claimed God rested on the Sabbath. Al-Alusi notes that no one can truly know God in His essence, but that the verse's aim is to affirm His greatness against polytheism. Al-Sha'rawi glosses qadr as measure, so the point is that they did not magnify God to the measure He deserves.

This verse states that God chooses messengers from among the angels, such as Jibril and Mika'il who carried revelation to the prophets, and from among humans, meaning the prophets He sends to His servants. Most commentators report that it was revealed in response to the polytheists who objected that the Reminder had been sent down to a man from among them. God answers that the choice is His alone and He selects whom He wills for the mission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "All-Hearing, All-Seeing" means He hears what the idolaters say and knows whom He chooses for His message. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi see it rather as a complete knowledge of all that can be heard and seen, and of the states of nations as they accept or reject the message. Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Sa'di add that the messengers are the elite of their kind, with pure souls, and that their selection proceeds from perfect knowledge. As for "what is before them and what is behind them", al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the Jalalayn take it to mean what came before the creation of the angels and messengers and what happens after their passing, al-Hasan takes it as their past and future deeds, and Yahya ibn Sallam as the hereafter and this world, while al-Razi distinguishes perfect knowledge from perfect power. The commentators agree that all affairs return to God, who is not questioned about what He does, unlike His creatures who are questioned, as al-Baydawi notes. The commentators do not settle between these different explanations.

This verse states that God chooses messengers from among the angels, such as Gabriel and Michael, and from among humans, meaning the prophets. He hears and sees all, and knows who is worthy of this mission. He also knows what lies before and behind His creatures, and all matters return to Him. Commentators offer several readings of "what is before them and what is behind them." Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and others take it to mean what they have done and what they will yet do. Ibn 'Isa understands it as what came before their creation and what comes after it, while Yahya ibn Sallam takes it as the affairs of the Hereafter and of this world. Most agree that the point is the all-encompassing knowledge of God over the past and future of beings, and the return of all matters to Him in the Hereafter. Al-Tabari reports that the verse was sent down in answer to the polytheists' question, "Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?" God replies that the choosing is His alone. Al-Razi draws from it that the angels are not gods, since their high rank comes from God's choice. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that God is not questioned about what He does, and no one may object to His choice of messengers. On the prostration of recitation at this verse, scholars differ: al-Shafi'i and Ahmad prescribe it here, while Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri do not, and Ibn Kathir and others offer no ruling between them.

This verse calls on the believers to bow (ruku') and prostrate (sujud), which most commentators take to mean prayer itself, since these two movements are its essential parts. It then orders them to worship their Lord alone and to do good, and it links success (falah) to this conduct. Al-Samani, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the good includes kinship ties, noble character and all forms of benevolence, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi understand the command as applying to what is not obligatory. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi see an order running from the specific to the general: prayer, then worship, then good deeds in general. Al-Zamakhshari reports that early Muslims sometimes prostrated without bowing, or the reverse, so the verse requires both. Al-Tabari understands success as obtaining what one seeks from God, whereas al-Biqa'i and al-Jawhari define it as triumph and lasting life in Paradise. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir note that the particle 'la'alla' expresses hope rather than doubt.

Scholars differ on whether this verse calls for a prostration of recitation. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq hold that it does, relying on the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir about the two prostrations of surah al-Hajj, which al-Tirmidhi considers weak. Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri hold that it does not, since the verse joins prostration with bowing. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi observe that the prostration here belongs to the prayer. On the nearby command to strive for God as is due to Him, al-Mawardi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that some, such as Ibn al-Mubarak, understand it as struggle against the self, and others see it as abrogated by the verse 'fear God as much as you can', while al-Razi concludes that it remains in force.

In this verse God commands the believers to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord and do good, in hope of success, and then to strive in God's cause with their full effort. Commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the phrase "as due to Him" as exerting all one's capacity, while Ibn Abbas adds that one should not fear the blame of anyone for God's sake, and Ibn al-Mubarak takes it as the struggle against the self and its desires. The verb "ijtaba" means to choose and single out. Most read "hardship" as narrowness, but al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya understand it as the concessions allowed: praying seated or shortened, deferring fasting while travelling, tayammum, and the repentance and expiations that open a way out of every sin. The phrase "the creed of your father Abraham" is read by some as an order to follow his religion, and by others as a comparison. On who named the Muslims, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir say it was God, in earlier scriptures and in the Quran, while Ibn Zayd, cited by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, ascribes it to Abraham on the basis of his prayer in al-Baqara; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the first view. The purpose is that the Messenger bear witness over you and that you bear witness over the nations that their messengers delivered the message. The verse ends with the command to establish prayer and give zakat and to hold fast to God, who is the best protector and the best helper.
